findings.evidence: Table 4-1, Economic constraints cell: "Infrastructure: ≈ $20/hour for an 8×H100 host at $2.50/GPU-hr on-demand [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]; not illustrative 2026 cloud-price input ($2.50/H100-GPU-hour, [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION], not a market fact) → $20/hr per 8-GPU node"
findings.issue: Prose defect: the clause "not illustrative 2026 cloud-price input" does not parse — it appears to be a merged/botched revision of "an illustrative 2026 cloud-price input" and "not a market fact", producing a self-contradictory fragment inside a dense table cell.
findings.fix_instruction: Rewrite the clause to read, e.g., "an illustrative 2026 cloud-price input ($2.50/H100-GPU-hour, [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION], not a market fact) → $20/hr per 8-GPU node".

findings.evidence: Page 78, Table 4-1 Economic constraints cell: "Basis first — full-utilization KV screen, no headroom, during active hours: at the ~6-host average the whole-fleet spend is ~$120/hour over the ~173.3 active hours/month (8 h × 260 workdays ÷ 12 = 173.3 h/mo; = $20,800/month), giving ~2.76M input and ~90K output tokens per $1 of fleet spend (active-hours basis)." Page 100 (§4.3): "~92,000 / 0.0333 ≈ ~2.76 million input tokens per $1 of fleet spend and ~3,000 / 0.0333 ≈ ~90,000 output tokens per $1".
findings.issue: The arithmetic 92,000/0.0333 = 2.762M checks, and 3,000/0.0333 = 90.09K checks. But the '$0.0333 per second' is derived from '$120/hour' = 120/3,600 = $0.03333/s — fine. The defect is that this ~2.76M-input-tokens-per-$1 figure is presented inside Table 4-1's Economic constraints cell, which is the workload-characterization table, with a long derivation embedded in a single cell (the cell also carries a second table's worth of content about API list prices, infrastructure price, and a note that the derived values are '[canonical scenario][DERIVED] per the table-level convention'). The table-level convention (p. 61) says a derived value carries [canonical scenario][DERIVED]; here the cell mixes an assumption ($1.20/$2.00 list price, [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]) with derived values inside one cell whose status is stated only in the trailing parenthetical — a reader scanning the cell cannot tell which number is which without the parenthetical at the end of a very long cell.
findings.fix_instruction: Split Table 4-1's Economic constraints cell into a short canonical value plus a footnote marker, and move the derivation (173.3 h, $20,800, 2.76M/$1, 90K/$1) into the derivation-notes block beneath the table where the other cells' derivations live, so status tags attach to individual numbers.

findings.evidence: Page 85 box rows: "Average arrival rate | ~10 rps [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] declared traffic input (2,000 users × one request ~every 200 s ≈ 10 rps) — declared, not derived ... The active-hours volume is ~6.24M requests/month (10 × 3,600 × 8 × 260/12 = 6,240,000)". Page 86: "Per-host monthly cost (reference) | ~$14.6K/host/mo on-demand (20 × 730 hr)". Page 87 sidebar: "Cloud, 6 hosts — active-hours basis (6 × 173.3 h × $20) | $20,800".
findings.issue: Recomputing the active-hours volume: 10 × 3,600 × 8 × 260 ÷ 12 = 6,240,000 — correct. Recomputing the active hours: 8 h × 260 workdays ÷ 12 = 173.33 h/mo — correct. Recomputing $20,800: 6 × 173.33 × $20 = $20,800 — correct. Recomputing the per-host monthly: 20 × 730 = $14,600 — correct. These all check. The defect is a stated-basis conflict the box itself creates: the box's 'Mean request service time' row says '~10 s [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] — an author-chosen round planning headline ... plus ~15% planning headroom to ~10 s', while the 'Execution occupancy' row uses Wexec ≈ 8.6 s. The book resolves this in the note beneath the box ('Do not use the ~10 s headline for occupancy'), but the two values are presented in the same authoritative box with no visual marker distinguishing 'planning headline, not for occupancy' from 'the value used for occupancy' inside the box itself — a reader who lifts a single row from the Canonical Workload box (as later chapters do, e.g. p. 118's '~10 s' appears in the Ch. 5 worked example at p. 121: 'the 7.08 s floor is 1.08 s prefill + 6.0 s decode') will carry the wrong W.
findings.fix_instruction: In the Canonical Workload box, add an explicit 'DO NOT USE FOR OCCUPANCY' flag (or split the row into 'Planning headline' and 'Occupancy service time') directly in the cell, so the two service-time values cannot be lifted out of context.

findings.evidence: Page 89 table rows: 'Cloud, 6 hosts — default paid-occupancy input | $87,600 | ≈ $14.04'; 'Cloud, 6 hosts — active-hours basis (6 × 173.3 h × $20) | $20,800 | ≈ $3.33'; 'Self-host — 21-host peak KV-screen fleet | $155,816.93 | ≈ $24.97'; 'Cloud, 21 hosts always-on at peak | $306,600 | ≈ $49.13'. Page 89 note: '* Peak-provisioned capacity ÷ average (10 rps) volume — a peak-capacity-cost-per-1K-average-volume-requests figure, not a per-request cost at either traffic level; at the 40 rps peak volume (24.96M requests/month) the same 21-host cloud total gives $306,600 ÷ 24,960K ≈ $12.28/1K.'
findings.issue: The book states 'quote ≈$3.33 per 1K requests (hour-matched) as the workload's per-1K unit cost' (p. 89) — yet the same page labels $14.04, $24.97 and $49.13 as 'capacity-cost artifacts'. But the $155,816.93 self-host row and the $306,600 always-on row are the rows that actually price the peak fleet (21 hosts), which is the fleet the canonical workload requires at its 40 rps peak; the $3.33 figure prices only the 6-host average fleet on the active-hours basis. So the book's declared 'unit cost' ($3.33) prices a fleet that cannot serve the peak, while the fleet that can serve the peak is labelled an artifact. The table's own framing ('the 21-host self-host total carries the same defect') does not resolve this: the defect is being attributed to the hour basis when the substantive issue is which fleet is being priced.
findings.fix_instruction: State explicitly which fleet each per-1K figure prices (average 6-host vs peak 21-host) in the table's first column, and change the unit-cost rule on p. 89 to name the fleet and traffic level it applies to (e.g. '≈$3.33/1K on the hour-matched active-hours basis for the 6-host average fleet') rather than presenting it as 'the workload's per-1K unit cost' unqualified.

findings.chapter: Ch. 4 Canonical Workload box — availability note
findings.evidence: Page 90: "Availability topology — UNPRICED / NOT VALIDATED in the canonical cost arithmetic. The canonical workload's operational constraint and SLA (this box: Multi-region deployment (active-active), 99.9% availability) state the requirement; the follow-on TCO and fleet arithmetic in Ch 16–17 prices a single-region deployment with N−1 single-host failover, not multi-region active-active. ... The canonical cost figures (Ch 16 $/1K req, Ch 17 host counts) therefore understate the cost of the canonical workload's own stated 99.9% availability requirement. Treat the TCO/fleet totals as single-region, N−1-only numbers, and add a separate multi-region capacity + replication cost line before the availability SLA can be considered met." Page 108 (§4.6): "Multi-region deployment (active-active) provides region-failure tolerance at an illustrative ~2× infrastructure cost (unvalidated — see caveat below)".
findings.issue: The box states the multi-region topology is 'UNPRICED / NOT VALIDATED' and that the TCO 'understates the cost of the canonical workload's own stated 99.9% availability requirement' — yet §4.6 (p. 108) states a '~2× infrastructure cost' for the same topology. That is a price, presented in the body without the UNPRICED qualifier in the same sentence (the qualifier arrives in the following sentence as 'this multi-region active-active topology and the 2× cost here are UNPRICED / NOT VALIDATED'). The chapter therefore simultaneously declares the topology unpriced and quotes a 2× multiplier for it, and the two statements live 18 pages apart with no cross-reference from the box to §4.6.
findings.fix_instruction: Add the 'UNPRICED / NOT VALIDATED' tag inline at the point the ~2× figure appears in §4.6 (not only in the trailing caveat), and add a back-reference in the Canonical Workload box's availability note to §4.6 so the two statements are visibly linked.

findings.evidence: Page 95: "2. Request completion time (service time W): the average end-to-end time from request submission to answer delivery. We deliberately keep TWO named values ... a planning round number of ~10 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill ~1.08 s + decode ~7.5 s ≈ 8.7 s, plus ~15% planning headroom to ~10 s — an author-chosen planning figure, not a measurement) versus the derived model-execution service time of ~8.6 s (prefill 1.08 s + decode 7.5 s, without the retrieval/plumbing term)".
findings.issue: Recompute the components: retrieval 0.12 s + prefill 1.08 s + decode 7.5 s = 8.70 s — correct. But the book then says the ~10 s headline includes '~15% planning headroom': 8.7 × 1.15 = 10.005 s — correct. However, the retrieval term: 8.70 − 0.12 = 8.58 s for Wexec, and 1.08 + 7.5 = 8.58 s — correct. The real defect is that ~1.08 s is the *budget cap* (a two-term upper reach, per Table 4-2 p. 94 and the Preface p. 19: 'the ~1.08 s prefill figure is a two-term-only upper reach, not a feasible deployed prefill target'), yet here it is used as if it were a modelled prefill runtime inside a service-time decomposition that then feeds Little's-law occupancy and, from there, the fleet sizing in Ch. 17 (p. 111: 'Wexec = 1.08 s prefill + 7.5 s decode = 8.58 s'). The book itself notes the modelled host prefill is ~0.47 s at 35% MFU (p. 79) — so the occupancy and every downstream host count are derived from a budget cap rather than a modelled or measured prefill time, without that being flagged at the point of use.
findings.fix_instruction: Add an explicit note in the Arithmetic Walk-Through step 2 (and in the Wexec definition carried into Ch. 7/16/17) that the 1.08 s prefill term is the two-term budget cap, not a modelled runtime, so Little's-law occupancy and the resulting host counts inherit that upper-bound status.

findings.evidence: Page 99: "The cap implies ≈8,500 tokens/s (9,200 ÷ 1.08 = 8,519): that is only the budget-implied single-request rate for a request that holds the whole host, not the modeled or measured prefill rate. The modeled host prefill is ~0.16 s at peak and ~0.47 s at 35% MFU, and the host's capacity screen is the ~19,800 tok/s sustained-planning rate at 35% MFU — a planning rate, not a ceiling. Eight GPUs are what make the cap reachable at all: one H100 sustains ~2,472 tok/s at 35% MFU."
findings.issue: Check the 8,519: 9,200 ÷ 1.08 = 8,518.5 — correct. Check the single-H100 35% MFU figure: 0.989 PFLOPS × 0.35 = 0.346 PFLOPS ÷ 140 GFLOP/token = 2,472 tok/s — correct, and 8 × 2,472 = 19,780 ≈ 19,800 — correct. The defect is the sentence 'Eight GPUs are what make the cap reachable at all': the modelled single-H100 prefill of 9,200 tokens at 35% MFU takes 9,200/2,472 = 3.72 s, and the 8-GPU host at 35% MFU takes ~0.47 s — both are well inside the 1.08 s cap, so the statement that eight GPUs are needed to make the cap 'reachable at all' is contradicted by the book's own numbers (one GPU at 35% MFU would take 3.72 s and fail, so at least two are needed — but the claim as written implies one GPU cannot reach it, which the book does not quantify). The sentence asserts a threshold the book never computes (the minimum GPU count to meet 1.08 s), while the numbers it supplies would allow it to be computed (⌈1.19 PFLOPS ÷ (0.989 × MFU)⌉).
findings.fix_instruction: Replace 'Eight GPUs are what make the cap reachable at all' with the computed minimum — e.g. 'at 35% MFU one H100 sustains ~2,472 tok/s, so a single GPU needs ~3.7 s for the 9.2K prefill; the 8-GPU host needs ~0.47 s — the minimum GPU count to meet the 1.08 s cap is ⌈1.19 PFLOPS ÷ (0.989 × 0.35)⌉ ≈ 4' — and state that the canonical 8-GPU choice is driven by concurrency and headroom, not by the cap alone.

findings.evidence: Page 100: "At the per-million rates, cost per request ≈ (9,200 × $1.20/1M) + (300 × $2.00/1M) = $0.01104 + $0.0006 = $0.01164 ≈ $0.012 per request". Page 106 (§4.6): "if the input token count could be reduced to 2 K (e.g. tighter retrieval/reranking to fewer chunks, context compression), or lower effective prefill cost for the same tokens (prefix caching, if priced favorably), the per-request API list cost falls from $0.01164 to ≈$0.0030 — the input leg goes from 9,200 × $1.20/1M = $0.01104 to 2,000 × $1.20/1M = $0.00240 while the output leg stays 300 × $2.00/1M = $0.0006, so the total moves $0.01164 → ≈$0.0030, a ~3.9× reduction ($0.01164 ÷ $0.0030 = 3.88)."
findings.issue: The arithmetic is correct: 9,200×1.20/1e6 = $0.01104; 300×2.00/1e6 = $0.0006; total $0.01164; 2,000×1.20/1e6 = $0.0024 + $0.0006 = $0.0030; ratio 3.88. The defect is that the Ch. 4 §4.6 'Architectural Consequence' bullet presents this as 'the lever the architect pulls when TCO is the binding constraint' — but the same chapter (p. 100) warns that this is 'a hosted-API figure and says nothing directly about fleet capacity' and that on the owned-fleet basis 'the same input reduction lowers prefill work and the KV footprint per request, which changes the host-count screen (Ch 17) — quantify that separately'. The consequence bullet then says 'On the owned-fleet basis the same input reduction lowers prefill work and the KV footprint per request, which changes the host-count screen (Ch 17) — quantify that separately on the fleet $/hr ÷ fleet rps basis, not from this $/request number.' So the chapter ends with a lever whose own-fleet effect is left unquantified and whose headline number (3.9×) is an API-basis figure that does not apply to the deployment the chapter is sizing. The 3.9× figure is the only quantified outcome in the bullet.
findings.fix_instruction: Add the owned-fleet quantification the bullet defers (e.g. the KV-screen host count at 2K input: 436 GB ÷ (2,300 × 2.62 MB) and the resulting Ch. 17 host count), so the consequence bullet does not leave a 'lever' whose decisive number comes from a different cost basis than the chapter's own fleet.

findings.evidence: Page 111: "nhosts = ⌈50 rps × 8.6 s / 17 slots⌉ = ⌈430/17⌉ = ⌈25.29⌉ = 26 hosts (full utilization) and on the u-only screen at a 70% target utilization the normative host-count form of Ch 17 Table 17-1 gives ⌈26 ÷ 0.70⌉ = ⌈37.14⌉ = 38 hosts (the occupancy cross-check ⌈430/(17 × 0.7)⌉ = ⌈430/11.9⌉ = ⌈36.13⌉ = 37 sits one host below it) — then 39 hosts before the spare, 40 under the book's provisioning policy, which multiplies the independent ρ = 0.95 as well and adds the N−1 reserve (⌈430/(17 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = ⌈430/11.305⌉ = ⌈38.04⌉ = 39; Ch 17 Table 17-1 adds +1 for the N−1 spare → 40)."
findings.issue: Two arithmetic checks fail. (a) ⌈430/11.9⌉ = ⌈36.13⌉ = 37 — correct. (b) ⌈430/11.305⌉ = ⌈38.04⌉ = 39 — 430/11.305 = 38.036, so ⌈38.04⌉ = 39 — correct. (c) But ⌈26 ÷ 0.665⌉ = ⌈39.10⌉ = 40 — 26/0.665 = 39.098, so ⌈39.10⌉ = 40 — correct. The problem is the sequence of statements: the text says the u-only screen gives '38 hosts', then 'then 39 hosts before the spare', then '40 under the book's provisioning policy'. But the ⌈26 ÷ 0.70⌉ = 38 figure already includes a 0.70 utilization derating, and the policy form ⌈26 ÷ (0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = 39 applies the reliability factor to the *full-utilization* host count (26), not to the already-derated 38. The text's own arithmetic produces two mutually inconsistent paths to the same answer: 26 ÷ 0.70 = 38 then +1 spare = 39, versus 26 ÷ 0.665 = 39 then +1 spare = 40. The book asserts these 'reproduce the normative result' without noting that they differ by one host in the middle step and only coincide at the end by construction of the ceil.
findings.fix_instruction: State the normative rule once (the host-count form: N = ⌈load ÷ C⌉, provisioned = ⌈N ÷ (u × ρ)⌉, working = provisioned − 1) and present the u-only and cross-check figures as named cross-checks, explicitly noting the one-host rounding artifact rather than presenting them as a sequence ('38 → 39 → 40') that reads as an incremental build-up.

findings.evidence: Page 111: "A prefill-throughput cross-check from the Chapter 8 model bounds it from below: 50 rps × 9,200 input = 460,000 prefill tokens/s ÷ ~19,800 tokens/s per host ... ≈ ~24 hosts (460,000 ÷ 19,800 = 23.23, ceiled to a whole host). (Do not divide by the ~8.5K tok/s single-request prefill rate, 9,200 ÷ 1.08 s — that is the rate for one request monopolizing a host, not a per-host aggregate, and using it here would be a unit error.)"
findings.issue: 460,000 ÷ 19,800 = 23.23 — correct, and the unit-error warning is correct. The defect is a register inconsistency: the Ch. 8 host prefill rate is described on p. 111 as 'the host's sustained-planning prefill rate' derived from '8 × ~2,472 tok/s at 35% MFU' — a planning rate explicitly 'not a ceiling' (p. 79, p. 111). But on p. 106 (Ch. 4 §4.6) the same ~19,800 tok/s is used to derive 'prefill alone needs ≥5 hosts at average' as though it were a capacity figure: 'at 10 rps the offered prefill load is ~92,000 tok/s against one host's ~19,800 tok/s sustained-planning rate, so prefill alone needs ≥5 hosts at average'. 92,000 ÷ 19,800 = 4.65 → ⌈⌉ = 5 — correct. The defect is the register language: a 'planning rate, not a ceiling' is used to produce a host count ('needs ≥5 hosts') without the caveat travelling with it, so the derived count reads as a capacity conclusion.
findings.fix_instruction: Carry the 'planning rate, not a ceiling' qualifier inline wherever the ~19,800 tok/s figure is used to derive a host count (Ch. 4 §4.6, Ch. 4 §4.8, Ch. 6 §6.8, Ch. 8), and mark the derived host counts as analytical bounds rather than capacity results.

findings.evidence: Page 106: "At 10 concurrent full-context requests the MHA figure is ~241 GB of KV on top of the 140 GB weights — 381 GB of the 640 GB pool — and the pool presses well before concurrency reaches 100 (~17 full-context requests once the ~64 GB runtime is reserved: 436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB ≈ 17.5, floored to 17 — the input-only 24.1 GB figure above would give 436 ÷ 24.1 ≈ 18 before the output tokens are counted)."
findings.issue: Recompute: 10 × 24.1 = 241 GB ✓; 241 + 140 = 381 GB ✓; 436 ÷ 24.9 = 17.51 → 17 ✓; 436 ÷ 24.1 = 18.09 → 18 ✓. The arithmetic is correct and the two bases are named. The defect is that the ~17 figure derived here (and in Ch. 7) is the per-host resident-slot ceiling, yet the sentence frames it as a property of the 640 GB *pool* with 'the pool presses well before concurrency reaches 100' — a pool-level statement, when the chapter's own Ch. 7 technical note (p. 171) establishes the per-rank bound as the binding one (99.97% full at 17.5 slots on an 80 GB rank). The p. 106 framing invites the reader to treat the 17 as a pool-level headroom statement.
findings.fix_instruction: Note in Ch. 4 §4.6 that the 17-slot ceiling is a per-host figure whose binding limit is per-rank (Ch. 7 §7.3 technical note), and add the pointer so the pool-level framing does not substitute for the per-rank test.

findings.evidence: Page 99: "p95 TTFT must stay ≤ 2 s — a tail ceiling above the 1.2 s target budget, allowing occasional cache misses or network jitter to land between the 1.2 s target and the 2 s ceiling." Page 106 (§4.6): "without admission scheduling, queued prefills can push p95 TTFT past the 2 s ceiling — chunked prefill and priority scheduling are the levers that address prefill/decode interference directly."
findings.issue: The book's canonical SLO pair is 'TTFT budget 1.2 s' with 'p95 TTFT ≤ 2 s'. These are two different numbers used for two different purposes (target vs tail ceiling), and the book consistently says so. The defect is that Ch. 6 (p. 132) and Ch. 6's Fig 6.2 use 'the 2 s SLO line' as *the* TTFT SLO when reading a request-latency distribution ('Under the canonical p95 TTFT SLO of ≤ 2 s'), while Ch. 4 uses 1.2 s as 'the TTFT budget' and 2 s as the p95 ceiling — and Ch. 2 (p. 42) lists 'TTFT budget 1.2 s' as the design budget with p95 ≤ 2 s as the SLO. A reader reading Ch. 6's Fig 6.2 against the 2 s line is judging against the tail ceiling, which the canonical box calls a 'budgeted ceiling' rather than a demonstrated value ('the demonstrated value under load requires an actual measurement', p. 79).
findings.fix_instruction: At each place the 2 s line is used as the pass/fail threshold for a measured distribution, name it 'the p95 TTFT ceiling (≤ 2 s)' and note that the 1.2 s figure is the design budget the tail ceiling relaxes, so the two thresholds are never silently swapped.

findings.evidence: Page 96: "4. Peak arrival rate: ~40 rps is the same behavior scaled to a burst/traffic spike — again a declared scenario input". Page 97: "The ~40 rps peak is assumed sustained over the provisioning burst interval — long enough for Little's Law and service-time occupancy to reach the modeled steady state (sustained for at least the service-time scale, Wexec ≈ 8.6 s — not a one-second or few-second spike), not a one-request 40-rps spike."
findings.issue: The two passages are consistent, but 'sustained for at least the service-time scale' (~8.6 s) is a very short window for a 'burst' against which a fleet is provisioned with N−1 and 70% × 95% headroom, and the book's own Ch. 6 mini-case (p. 141) uses the 40 rps peak as the sizing point for the whole fleet. The defect is that Ch. 4 never states a burst *duration* — 'assumed sustained over the provisioning burst interval' leaves the interval undefined, so the fleet sizing in Ch. 17 (which provisions for the peak with headroom and failover) cannot be checked against any burst-length assumption, and the difference between the 'peak' and 'average' fleet sizes (6 vs 21 hosts) is unfalsifiable without it.
findings.fix_instruction: Add an explicit burst-duration assumption to the canonical workload (e.g. 'the 40 rps peak is sustained for up to N minutes') with a provenance tag, so the peak-fleet sizing in Ch. 17 has a stated time basis.

findings.evidence: Page 107, Fig 4.1: the diagram maps each of the six workload dimensions to an architectural decision, with the caption: 'Each arrow means the dimension constrains/informs the corresponding architectural choice — it is a heuristic influence, not a deterministic one-to-one mapping. The arrows are non-exclusive: in practice a dimension often influences several decisions at once (e.g. latency SLO shapes both model choice and serving configuration), and the six axes are a starting lens, not a partition. [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]'
findings.issue: The figure draws six one-to-one arrows (each dimension pointing at exactly one decision) while its caption says the mapping is not one-to-one and that 'a dimension often influences several decisions at once'. The caption therefore disclaims the very structure the figure draws. The chapter's own worked example contradicts the one-to-one mapping: §4.6 shows the token profile driving model selection, KV sizing, serving configuration and the fleet screen simultaneously, and §4.3 shows the latency SLO driving both model choice and serving configuration.
findings.fix_instruction: Either add secondary arrows to Fig 4.1 for the multi-influence cases the caption names (latency SLO → model choice and serving configuration; token profile → KV sizing and prefill demand), or change the caption to say the figure shows one representative influence per dimension rather than claiming to depict the mapping.

findings.evidence: Page 100: "Cost per request: At 10 rps, each request carries ~9,500 tokens (9,200 input + 300 output). At the per-million rates, cost per request ≈ (9,200 × $1.20/1M) + (300 × $2.00/1M) = $0.01164 ≈ $0.012 per request per inference cycle". Page 101: "On the active-hours basis (~$120/hr × 173.3 active h/mo = $20,800/mo ÷ 6.24M requests) the same fleet is ~$3.33 per 1K requests, i.e. ~$0.0033 per request — the same value the full-util formula gives, because both divide an hour-matched spend by an hour-matched volume."
findings.issue: Check the two: $0.01164 (API list-price basis) vs $0.0033 (owned-fleet full-util basis). The chapter states these are different bases and warns against conflating them. The arithmetic is right (20,800/6,240 = $3.333 per 1K ✓). The defect is that the canonical workload's own stated cost position is never reconciled against the two numbers: the workload's economic constraint (Table 4-1) is expressed as a tokens-per-dollar figure (~2.76M input tokens per $1 of fleet spend), which is a third basis again. A reader of Ch. 4 encounters three per-request/per-dollar numbers for the same canonical workload ($0.012, $0.0033, $0.014) with the chapter's careful basis notes, but the economic-constraint cell of the canonical table quotes the fourth figure, and no single place states which of them is the workload's economic constraint for comparison against the managed-API alternative.
findings.fix_instruction: Add a short reconciliation paragraph (or a single column in the cost-basis table) that states, for the canonical workload, the four figures side by side with their bases and one sentence on which one should be compared with which — 'compare owned-fleet $/request against owned-fleet $/request; compare API $/request against API $/request; never across' — and name which figure the workload's own budget ceiling should be written against.
